title: A Loop That Never Allocates: A Fixed Pool, and What It Costs to Lend and Take Back

questions.question: A control loop makes a message with new each pass and frees it at the end of the pass. It does not leak. What is the problem?
options: It still allocates, and how long the heap takes depends on everything that ran before, so the loop's time is not under its control
questions.explanation: A leak check passes and the loop can still miss its deadline.

questions.question: How many heap allocations did 100000 lend and take back cycles make through the pool, and through new?
options: 0 through the pool and 100000 through new
questions.explanation: The count is of every allocation the program makes.

questions.question: The pool has all sixty-four messages out and is asked for a sixty-fifth. What should it do?
options: Wrap round and lend the oldest
Return nullptr, and let the caller decide what to do
questions.explanation: A pool that wraps round lends a message someone is still using.

questions.question: Why is a second release of the same message refused?
options: The slot would be on the free stack twice and be lent to two users
questions.explanation: After the refused double release, 64 lends still gave 64 different messages.

questions.question: Why is the most recently returned slot the next one lent?
options: It is on top of the stack, and it was used a moment ago, so its memory is the most likely to be in the cache
questions.explanation: The suite checks that the same slot came back, clean.

questions.question: What is a pool NOT a solution to?
options: A message used after it was released: a raw pointer to a slot can still be used by a caller who has given it back
questions.explanation: Wrap the lend in an object that returns it, as lesson 02-03 did.
